passages.happening:
Paul turns to his own preaching as proof of what he has just said.

“When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with eloquence or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony about God” (verse 1). “For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified” (verse 2).

He did not arrive as a confident performer. “I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling” (verse 3).

His message did not depend on clever speech. It was “not with persuasive words of wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power” (verse 4). And he gives the reason: “so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Paul had come to Corinth after a hard few months. Acts tells of a beating and jail in Philippi, of being driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, and of a cool hearing in Athens (Acts 16 to 17). In Corinth he began alone, working with his hands as a tentmaker beside Aquila and Priscilla. Acts says the Lord spoke to him in a vision at night: “Do not be afraid” (Acts 18:9). So his ‘weakness and fear’ were real.

A travelling speaker in a Greek city was expected to make an impression. Orators performed, displayed their learning, and gathered fans and fees. Paul chose another way. He supported himself by hand work, which many educated people looked down on, and he spoke plainly.

Paul's resolve to know nothing but Christ crucified does not mean Paul stopped thinking about anything else. His letters cover marriage, food, worship, money and the end of the world. It means he chose a centre. Everything else he taught would be measured by the cross.

‘Demonstration’ is the Greek apodeixis. Speakers used it for a convincing proof in an argument. Paul's proof was of another kind: the Spirit at work, changing people.

One small point about verse 1. Old copies of the letter differ here. Some read that Paul proclaimed ‘the testimony’ of God, and others ‘the mystery’ of God. The Berean Standard Bible follows ‘testimony’. Either way the content is the same: God's plan, shown in the crucified Christ.
passages.ot:
Paul's resolve to boast only in the crucified Christ follows from the words of Jeremiah he quoted just before, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1:31). Jeremiah had said the wise, the strong and the rich must not boast in themselves (Jeremiah 9:23).

The Old Testament often shows God working through a messenger who feels weak. Moses protested, “I am slow of speech and tongue” (Exodus 4:10). Jeremiah said, “I surely do not know how to speak” (Jeremiah 1:6). In both cases God sent them anyway, and the power was his.
passages.asks: Paul trusted the message more than his own skill. Ask what your faith rests on: a gifted speaker, a good argument, a strong feeling, or God's power. Ask, too, whether weakness and fear have kept you from speaking about Christ. Paul was afraid in Corinth, and God used him there.

passages.happening:
Paul does not say the gospel has no wisdom at all. “Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom” (verse 6). But it is “not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing” (verse 6).

“No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began” (verse 7).

“None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (verse 8).

Then he quotes Scripture: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
‘Mature’ is the Greek teleios, complete or grown up. Some Corinthians probably thought of themselves as the mature ones, above ordinary believers. Paul uses their word, but in the next chapter he will tell them they are still infants (3:1).

‘Mysterious and hidden’ wisdom means something God kept hidden and has now made known. For Paul a ‘mystery’ is not a secret kept for a few insiders. It is God's plan, once hidden, now told openly to all: that he would save the world through a crucified Messiah.

Who are ‘the rulers of this age’ who crucified the Lord? Readers answer in three ways. Many take them as the human rulers who put Jesus to death: Pilate, Herod and the temple leaders. Others take them as spiritual powers standing behind human rulers, since Paul elsewhere speaks of rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms (Ephesians 6:12). Some hold both together. On every reading, the rulers thought they had won, and the cross was their undoing.

‘The Lord of glory’ is a striking title for a crucified man. In the Bible, glory belongs to God. Paul gives that title to the one the rulers nailed to a cross. That is the hidden wisdom: the one the world shamed was the Lord of glory all along.
passages.ot:
The quotation in verse 9 is a puzzle, and it is best stated honestly. Paul introduces it with ‘as it is written’, the formula he uses for Scripture. But no verse of the Old Testament says exactly these words.

The closest is Isaiah 64:4: “From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him” (Isaiah 64:4). The ideas are the same: no ear has heard, no eye has seen, God acts for his people. But the wording differs, and Isaiah speaks of those who ‘wait for Him’ where Paul has ‘those who love Him’.

Readers explain this in several ways. Most think Paul gives Isaiah 64:4 freely, perhaps from memory, mixed with phrases from nearby verses, such as Isaiah 65:17, where the former things will not “come to mind” (Isaiah 65:17), and Isaiah 52:15. Already in the early church some readers thought the words came from another Jewish book, now lost. No one can be sure. What is clear is Paul's point, and it is Isaiah's point too: God's plan is beyond what anyone could see or imagine, until God shows it.

‘The rulers of this age’ who opposed the Lord echo the psalm in which “the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2). The first Christians read that psalm of the rulers who crucified Jesus (Acts 4:25-27).
passages.hard: Verse 9 is often heard as a promise about heaven: no one can imagine what God has prepared. That is a true hope, and Paul shares it. But in its place here the verse says more than that. Paul is talking about God's wisdom in the cross, hidden from the rulers and now revealed. The very next verse says, “But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit” (verse 10). What no eye had seen, God has now shown. So the verse is not only about the life to come. It is about what God has already made known in Christ.
passages.asks: The rulers looked at Jesus on the cross and saw a defeated man. Ask what the world around you counts as weakness or failure that God may see very differently. Ask whether you have ever been surprised by God's ways, and what it would mean to let him surprise you again.

passages.t: Taught by the Spirit, and ‘the mind of Christ’
passages.happening:
“But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (verse 10).

Paul gives a picture. No one knows a person's thoughts except that person's own spirit. In the same way, “no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God” (verse 11).

Believers have received the Spirit who is from God, “that we may understand what God has freely given us” (verse 12). So Paul speaks “in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words” (verse 13).

“The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned” (verse 14). But the spiritual person can judge all things (verse 15).

Paul ends with a question from Scripture and a bold claim: “‘For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct Him?’ But we have the mind of Christ” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Two Greek words are set side by side here. ‘Natural’ is psychikos, from psychē, soul or life. It describes a person living only by ordinary human powers, without the Spirit of God. It does not mean wicked. It means limited: like trying to hear music with no ears for it. ‘Spiritual’ is pneumatikos, a person shaped by the Spirit of God.

The Corinthians liked the word ‘spiritual’. Some seem to have used it to rank themselves above other believers. Paul does not say there are two classes of Christian. Anyone who has received the Spirit can receive what God gives. In chapter 3 he will tell the proud Corinthians that, judging by their quarrels, they are not living like spiritual people at all.

Verse 15, the spiritual person ‘is not subject to anyone’s judgment’, is easily misused. It is not a licence for anyone to say, ‘No one can correct me.’ Paul spends the whole letter correcting people who thought they were spiritual. He means that the world's way of judging cannot measure the things of God.

Verse 11 also says something about the Spirit. The Spirit knows God's thoughts as a person's own spirit knows his. Christians have long read this as showing that the Spirit is not a mere force but is himself God, knowing God from within.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Isaiah 40:13. In the Hebrew, as the Berean Standard Bible translates it, Isaiah asks, “Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?” (Isaiah 40:13). Paul's wording, “who has known the mind of the Lord” (verse 16), is close to the old Greek translation, which has ‘mind’ where the Hebrew has ‘Spirit’. In Isaiah the question expects the answer ‘no one’. No one can advise God. Paul agrees, and then adds his surprise: through the Spirit, believers have been given the mind of Christ, who is Lord.

Paul uses the same verse again in Romans, in his hymn to God's wisdom: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:34).

The idea that God's Spirit gives understanding runs back through the prophets. God promised through Ezekiel, “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).
passages.hard:
‘We have the mind of Christ’ (verse 16). Does this mean believers know everything, or can never be wrong?

No. Paul spends this whole letter correcting believers who were sure they knew. He also says, “Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror” (13:12). ‘The mind of Christ’ is not a claim to private knowledge. It is a way of thinking shaped by the crucified Lord. Paul describes it elsewhere: Christ “humbled Himself and became obedient to death” (Philippians 2:8). To have his mind is to see the world from the foot of the cross, to value what he valued, and to give yourself for others as he did.

And the ‘we’ is plural. Paul is speaking of the church together, listening to the Spirit together, not of one person who claims to have a hotline to God.
passages.asks: Paul says the things of God are understood only by the Spirit. Ask God's Spirit to teach you as you read Scripture, rather than reading only for facts. Then ask what ‘the mind of Christ’ would change in a decision you face this week, if you saw it from the foot of the cross.
